assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks turned the magic-wavelength idea into the most precise measurement instruments ever built, with fractional uncertainties near 1e-18. This is the kind of advance that moves what can be measured and how precisely: new tests of fundamental constants and relativity, relativistic geodesy, and a path to redefining the second. Experimentally concrete, with clear linewidth and systematics budgets.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept (2001-2003) and made the first Sr lattice clock; Ye drove it to the 1e-18 level and combined it with frequency-comb and cavity-stabilization work. Two laureates is a clean configuration. Others (e.g. Lemonde, Takamoto, ion-clock groups, Hall and Hansch already recognised for combs) may be cited for adjacent work. Hall and Hansch already received the 2005 prize for frequency combs; the lattice contribution is distinct.
assessment.maturity: Independently confirmed by many groups (JILA, RIKEN, NIST, PTB, SYRTE, NPL and others) with Sr, Yb and Hg. Redefinition of the second is under discussion, which supports timely recognition. Interpretation is stable.
uncertainties: Whether to also credit ion-clock work (Wineland/Rosenband, Al+ clocks) is open; Wineland was recognised in 2012 for ion control.
Exact priority split between Katori's proposal and Ye's accuracy demonstrations is from memory, not verified here.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Single-spin optical readout and coherent control of NV and related colour centres created a room-temperature solid-state qubit and a new class of nanoscale sensors for magnetic field, electric field, temperature and strain, used from condensed-matter imaging to biology. It is both a measurement technique that opened a field and a quantum-information platform. Wide downstream use.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup demonstrated optical detection of single NV spins (1997) and coherent control; Awschalom led coherent control, SiC/diamond defect qubits and spintronics integration; Lukin contributed quantum sensing and nanoscale NMR and networking proposals with Walsworth and colleagues. Walsworth is a fourth credited name; three is the limit and Awschalom, Wrachtrup and Lukin appear most decisive but others (Jelezko, Hanson, Gruber, Maze, Taylor) are not on the supplied list.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced extensively worldwide; commercial sensors exist. Mature on the physics, while applications such as biology sensing and networks remain developing.
uncertainties: Attribution is diffuse: Jelezko, Gruber, Hanson, Maze and Taylor are not in the credited names and are arguably decisive.
Compound discovery (qubit, sensor, quantum network) may need distinct recognition.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller proposal (1995) for trapped-ion quantum gates, followed by the experimental demonstration of gates, entanglement and algorithms in ion chains, established a leading platform for quantum computing. Long coherence times and high gate fidelities are the benchmark against which other platforms are measured. I value that this combines a clear proposal and decisive experiments.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller made the theoretical proposal; Blatt's group realised the Cirac-Zoller gate and many multi-ion entanglement experiments. Wineland and Monroe are not on the list, and Wineland already won in 2012 for ion control, which complicates the story. The three names form a coherent theory-plus-experiment configuration, but a fair prize may also need to consider Monroe, Wineland group gates or Molmer-Sorensen.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed by multiple groups (Innsbruck, NIST, Oxford, Maryland, Quantinuum, IonQ). Scalable systems are being built; the prize timing is plausible but the relation to the 2012 prize is a concern.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2012 prize (Wineland) and omission of Monroe and Wineland-group gate work.
Overlap with ballot B047, a closely related candidate; I treat only one.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED created the architecture for strong coupling, dispersive readout and control of superconducting qubits, which underlies nearly all modern superconducting quantum processors. Clear experiments with measurable coupling strengths and coherence, high impact on both quantum information and sensing of microwave photons.
assessment.attribution: Blais proposed circuit QED (2004) with Huang, Wallraff, Girvin and Schoelkopf; Wallraff and Schoelkopf demonstrated strong coupling in 2004 and developed it. Girvin and Huang are not credited here, which may leave attribution incomplete. Given the 2025 prize to Clarke, Devoret and Martinis for macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits, a second superconducting-circuit prize so soon is a concern.
assessment.maturity: Mature and independently reproduced in many labs and companies; the interpretation is stable.
uncertainties: Recency of the 2025 prize on superconducting circuits may make another circuit prize premature.
Girvin, who co-authored the original proposal, is not among the credited names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Programmable arrays of individually trapped Rydberg atoms, using optical tweezers, gave a platform for quantum simulation and gates with up to hundreds of qubits, and recent error-corrected logical operations. Technically impressive and fast moving, building on the Rydberg blockade ideas from Jaksch, Cirac, Zoller and Lukin.
assessment.attribution: Saffman contributed the blockade-gate proposals and demonstrations, Browaeys the tweezer-array realisation and blockade experiments, Lukin the large-scale programmable arrays and simulation. Zoller is credited here but his contribution is theoretical and I chose three experimentally decisive names. Other groups (Bloch, Ahn, Endres, Weiss, Regal-related tweezers) are not listed.
assessment.maturity: Rapidly maturing but still young; large-scale fault tolerance is not yet established, so recognition is possibly premature.
uncertainties: Premature relative to the pace of the field; the benchmark results may be superseded.
Other groups (Ahn, Bloch, Endres, Kaufman) are not in the credited names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice quantum simulation, from the superfluid to Mott insulator transition (Greiner, Bloch, Hansch) and later quantum gas microscopes, realised controllable many-body Hamiltonians and allowed direct observation of individual atoms. A strong demonstration that carefully controlled atomic systems can answer questions in condensed-matter physics.
assessment.attribution: Jaksch and Zoller proposed the Bose-Hubbard realisation in optical lattices; Greiner and Bloch performed the Mott transition experiments and the single-site imaging. Cirac is also credited but I prefer a configuration anchored in the proposal and the experiments. Hansch, the senior author of the Mott experiment, and Jaksch are not credited, and Hansch has already received the prize.
assessment.maturity: Well established and reproduced widely; quantum gas microscopes are standard. The platform is mature, though the claim of quantum advantage in simulation is still developing.
uncertainties: Omission of Jaksch and Hansch from the credited names affects fairness.
Overlap with the 2001 and 2005 AMO prizes in the broader community.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ti:sapphire and semiconductor saturable absorber mirror (SESAM) mode-locked solid-state lasers made compact, reliable femtosecond sources that underlie ultrafast spectroscopy, frequency combs and attosecond science. A true instrumentation advance that enabled a great deal of other measurement work.
assessment.attribution: Moulton developed Ti:sapphire as a laser medium; Sibbett demonstrated Kerr-lens mode-locking; Keller developed SESAMs enabling robust self-starting mode-locking. Spence and others are not on the list. This is a plausible three-way split between gain medium, mode-locking and passive mode-locking.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature, with decades of widespread use. Recognition could be considered overdue, though adjacent prizes (2018 chirped-pulse amplification, 2005 combs, 2023 attosecond) already cover much of the application area.
uncertainties: Adjacent recent prizes (2018, 2023) may reduce the committee's appetite.
Exact credit among Moulton, Sibbett, Spence and Keller is from memory and not verified here.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Pulsar timing arrays reached evidence for a nanohertz gravitational-wave background in 2023, a measurement requiring decades of precise timing of millisecond pulsars and careful noise modelling. It opens a new gravitational-wave band. As a measurement achievement it is impressive.
assessment.attribution: Attribution is hard: the result is a collaborative effort (NANOGrav, EPTA, PPTA, CPTA, InPTA) and the credited names represent consortium leadership rather than discovery of a single effect. Manchester led PPTA, Kramer EPTA, McLaughlin NANOGrav. A fair three-person split across consortia is conceivable but arbitrary.
assessment.maturity: Evidence is at roughly 3-4 sigma, with an astrophysical origin (supermassive black hole binaries versus new physics) not yet settled. Recognition is likely premature.
uncertainties: Significance is below conventional discovery thresholds and the source is unresolved.
Large-collaboration attribution; the three named people may not capture decisive contributions.
